Emims
EE-mims
n. pl.
Hebrew Emim, terrors or terrible ones, from the root ayom, dreadful. The name is not what they called themselves but what their neighbours called them: the Moabites call them Emims (Deuteronomy 2:11). A whole people known to history only by the fear they produced.

Biblical Definition

The Emims were the aboriginal inhabitants of the plateau that afterward belonged to Moab, and Scripture describes them in the same breath as the Anakims: a people great, and many, and tall (Deuteronomy 2:10), accounted giants. They appear once in the narrative of Abraham’s day, when Chedorlaomer and the eastern kings swept down the King’s Highway and smote the Rephaims in Ashteroth Karnaim, and the Zuzims in Ham, and the Emims in Shaveh Kiriathaim (Genesis 14:5). After that they are gone, and Moab holds their country. Moses rehearses this to Israel for a particular purpose. As the nation came up the east side of the Dead Sea, God forbade them to touch Moab: Distress not the Moabites, neither contend with them in battle… because I have given Ar unto the children of Lot for a possession (Deuteronomy 2:9). Then, parenthetically, He tells them who used to live there and what became of them. Israel was about to face the Anakims in Canaan and was terrified of them; Moses answers the fear by pointing across the valley and observing that a people just as tall once held that ground, and Lot’s children hold it now, and God arranged the transfer. The giants of Canaan are not an argument against the promise. They are its ordinary raw material.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 has no EMIM entry. The Hebrew name means terrors, and the Authorized Version transliterates it in the plural as Emims, keeping the Hebrew plural ending rather than anglicizing it.

expand to see more

EMIMS, n. pl. — Terrible ones; the ancient giant people of the land afterward held by Moab, east of the Dead Sea.

The Hebrew plural -im is retained in the English of the Authorized Version, as with Anakims, Rephaims, Zamzummims, and Zuzims.

The name is descriptive rather than tribal: what their neighbours called them for the terror they inspired (Deuteronomy 2:11).

They are reckoned with the Rephaim, the general Old Testament designation for the tall peoples of the land before Israel.

Webster 1828 does not treat these transliterations; the sense comes wholly from Genesis 14 and Deuteronomy 2.

Key Scripture

Genesis 14:5 — "And in the fourteenth year came Chedorlaomer, and the kings that were with him, and smote the Rephaims in Ashteroth Karnaim, and the Zuzims in Ham, and the Emims in Shaveh Kiriathaim,"

Deuteronomy 2:9 — "And the LORD said unto me, Distress not the Moabites, neither contend with them in battle: for I will not give thee of their land for a possession; because I have given Ar unto the children of Lot for a possession."

Deuteronomy 2:10 — "The Emims dwelt therein in times past, a people great, and many, and tall, as the Anakims;"

Deuteronomy 2:11 — "Which also were accounted giants, as the Anakims; but the Moabites call them Emims."

Acts 17:26 — "And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation;"

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Moses’ own use of the Emims: God removes giants routinely, and a believer’s fear of what is large is answered by history, not by flattery.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The recovery here is a method of pastoral encouragement that has almost disappeared. Israel’s fear at Kadeshbarnea was specific: the cities are great and walled up to heaven; and moreover we have seen the sons of the Anakims there. Moses does not answer that fear by telling Israel she is stronger than she thinks. He answers it by recounting what God did to the Emims, the Zamzummims, and the Horims — three peoples every bit as tall, every one of them dispossessed, and none of them by Israel. The encouragement is entirely about God’s ordinary practice, and not at all about Israel’s capacity. Modern exhortation almost always inverts this, and produces a courage that collapses the moment the walls are actually seen.

The second thing to name is the humility of the record. A people great, many, and tall held a fertile plateau for generations and left no monument in Scripture except a name meaning terrors, given them by someone else. Their walls came down, their cities passed to Lot’s children, and the whole account occupies two verses in a parenthesis. Nations do not read their own obituaries. The Christian who takes this seriously will hold his own age’s permanence loosely, and will not be greatly impressed by anything merely large.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Emim (H368), terrors, terrible ones, from ayom (H366), dreadful; reckoned among the Rephaim (H7497), the giants.

expand to see more

Hebrew Emim (H368) — the Emims; terrors, from the root for dread.

Hebrew ayom (H366) — terrible, dreadful; used of the beloved in Song of Solomon 6:4 and of the Chaldeans in Habakkuk 1:7.

Hebrew Rephaim (H7497) — the giants; the general class in which Deuteronomy 2:11 reckons the Emims.

Hebrew Anaqim (H6062) — the Anakims; the standard of size against which the Emims are measured.

Hebrew Shaveh Qiryathayim — the plain of Kiriathaim, where Chedorlaomer smote them (Genesis 14:5).

Usage

"A people great, and many, and tall, as the Anakims (Deuteronomy 2:10) — the measure of what God had already removed."

"The Moabites call them Emims (Deuteronomy 2:11) — a nation remembered only by the fear it caused."

"Smote… the Emims in Shaveh Kiriathaim (Genesis 14:5) — their single appearance in the narrative."
